terms.definition: A container above subscriptions for applying Azure Policy and RBAC to many subscriptions at once; up to six levels deep under the tenant root group.
A billing and access boundary that holds resource groups; quotas and many limits apply per subscription.
A logical container for resources that share a lifecycle; deleting it deletes everything in it.
The deployment and management layer of Azure: every portal, CLI, PowerShell and template request goes through it.
Azure role-based access control: who (security principal) can do what (role definition) where (scope), through a role assignment.
The binding of a role definition to a security principal at a scope; it inherits to every child scope.
An Entra ID identity Azure manages for a resource, so code can get tokens without any stored secret. System-assigned lives and dies with the resource; user-assigned is standalone.
The identity of an application in a tenant; what a pipeline or app signs in as.
Microsoft's cloud identity service (formerly Azure Active Directory): users, groups, app registrations and sign-in.
Entra ID policies that grant, block or require MFA for sign-ins based on user, app, location, device and risk.
A service that evaluates resources against rules and can deny, audit, modify or deploy to enforce standards - for everyone, Owners included.
A group of policy definitions assigned together (a policy set), such as a compliance benchmark.
CanNotDelete or ReadOnly protection on a scope that overrides permissions until the lock is removed.
A name/value pair on a resource or group, used for cost allocation, automation and governance. Tags do not inherit by default.
A pre-configured, governed environment (management groups, policies, networking, identity) that workloads are deployed into.
A private network in Azure (VNet) with your own address space, split into subnets.
A range of a VNet's address space; Azure reserves 5 addresses in every subnet.
Network security group: stateful allow/deny rules by priority, applied to subnets and NICs.
Application security group: a label for NICs so NSG rules can target roles (web, db) instead of IP addresses.
A Microsoft-maintained group of IP prefixes (e.g. Storage, AzureLoadBalancer) usable in NSG and firewall rules.
A low-latency private link between two VNets; it is not transitive.
A NIC with a private IP in your subnet that maps to one PaaS resource; pair it with a private DNS zone.
Extends a subnet's identity to a PaaS service over the Azure backbone; the service keeps its public IP.
An Azure DNS zone resolvable only from linked VNets, e.g. privatelink.blob.core.windows.net for private endpoints.
Encrypted site-to-site or point-to-site connectivity over the internet into a VNet.
A private, dedicated connection from on-premises to Microsoft through a connectivity provider.
Managed RDP/SSH to VMs over TLS from the portal or native client, without public IPs on the VMs.
Layer-4 (TCP/UDP) load balancing within a region; Standard SKU is zone-redundant and secure by default.
A regional layer-7 (HTTP) load balancer with path-based routing, TLS termination and an optional WAF.
Web application firewall: blocks common web attacks (OWASP rules) on Application Gateway or Front Door.
A global layer-7 entry point with anycast, caching, TLS and health-based failover between regions.
DNS-based global traffic routing (priority, weighted, performance, geographic).
Gives a subnet's outbound traffic a fixed public IP and many SNAT ports.
A custom route in a route table that overrides Azure's system routes, e.g. to send traffic through a firewall.
The container for blobs, files, queues and tables, with one redundancy and performance setting.
Locally redundant storage: three copies in one datacentre.
Zone-redundant storage: three copies across availability zones in one region.
Geo-redundant storage: LRS plus an asynchronous copy in the paired region (RA-GRS lets you read it).
Hot, Cool, Cold or Archive pricing for blobs: cheaper storage costs more to read.
Shared access signature: a signed URL granting limited, time-bound access to storage. Prefer user delegation SAS.
Storage rules that tier or delete blobs by age automatically.
Keeps deleted blobs, containers, shares or vaults recoverable for a retention period.
Managed SMB/NFS file shares; Azure File Sync caches them on Windows servers.
A physically separate datacentre group within a region with its own power, cooling and network.
Two regions in the same geography that Azure pairs for staged updates and geo-replication.
Spreads VMs across fault and update domains in one datacentre (99.95% SLA).
Groups of identical VMs that autoscale and upgrade together.
The compute (SKU and instance count) that App Service apps run on.
A live staging copy of an App Service app you can swap into production with no downtime.
Azure Kubernetes Service: managed Kubernetes control plane; you run node pools and workloads.
Azure Container Registry: private registry for container images and OCI artifacts.
Serverless containers on Kubernetes with scale-to-zero, revisions and ingress, without managing a cluster.
The platform for metrics, logs, alerts and insights across Azure.
Where Azure Monitor logs are stored and queried with KQL.
Kusto Query Language: a pipe-based read-only query language for Log Analytics, Application Insights and Data Explorer.
Application performance monitoring: requests, dependencies, exceptions and traces from your code.
Per-resource configuration that streams platform logs and metrics to Log Analytics, storage or Event Hubs.
Who and what an alert notifies or triggers: email, SMS, webhook, Logic App, ITSM.
Managed backup for VMs, files, databases and blobs into a Recovery Services or Backup vault.
Replicates VMs to another region for disaster recovery failover.
Recovery point objective: how much data you can afford to lose, measured in time.
Recovery time objective: how long you can afford to be down.
Service level agreement: the availability Microsoft commits to (and credits if missed) for a service.
Managed store for secrets, keys and certificates; use the Azure RBAC permission model and managed identities.
Trusting an external token (GitHub Actions, Kubernetes) instead of a secret: OIDC tokens are exchanged for Entra ID tokens.
Cloud security posture management and workload protection: secure score, recommendations and threat detection.
Static application security testing: scanning source code for vulnerabilities in the pipeline.
Software composition analysis: finding vulnerable or badly licensed dependencies.
Software bill of materials: the list of components inside a build, for supply-chain security.
Merging and building every change automatically, with tests, so problems surface early.
Every change that passes the pipeline is releasable; deployment is a button (or automatic, for continuous deployment).
An Azure Pipelines definition kept in the repository: trigger, stages, jobs and steps.
The machine that runs pipeline jobs: Microsoft-hosted, self-hosted, scale set or Managed DevOps Pools.
Azure DevOps' stored connection to an external service such as an Azure subscription; prefer workload identity federation.
An Azure Pipelines target (with deployment history) where approvals and checks are configured.
Gates on an environment or resource that a deployment must pass: manual approval, business hours, Azure Monitor alerts.
Package feeds (NuGet, npm, Maven, Python, Universal) with upstream sources and views for promotion.
MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: breaking, feature, fix.
Rules on a protected branch: required reviewers, linked work items, build validation, comment resolution.
A proposed change reviewed and validated before merging into a protected branch.
Everyone integrates into one main branch frequently, with short-lived branches and feature flags.
A branching model with develop, feature, release and hotfix branches around main.
A runtime switch that turns functionality on or off without a deployment.
Two production environments; deploy to the idle one, then switch traffic.
Send a small share of real traffic to the new version and watch it before going wider.
Defining infrastructure in versioned, reviewable files (Bicep, ARM, Terraform) instead of clicking.
A concise language that compiles to ARM templates, with modules, type safety and implicit dependencies.
Terraform's record mapping configuration to real resources; keep it in a locked remote backend.
Differences between what IaC defines and what actually exists, usually from manual changes.
Deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore - the four delivery performance measures.
